title: Prop 19 Explained: Move at 55+ Without Losing Your Tax Base
description: Over 55 in California? Prop 19 may let you move anywhere in the state and keep much of your property tax base. Here's how it works and how to plan the loan.
image_alt: Stack of worn cardboard moving boxes near a window, lit by strong sunlight

faq.q: Who qualifies for a Prop 19 base year value transfer?
faq.a: Homeowners 55 or older when they sell their original home, severely disabled homeowners, and victims of a Governor-declared wildfire or natural disaster may qualify, as long as both homes are principal residences.

faq.q: Can I buy a more expensive home and still use Prop 19?
faq.a: Yes. If the replacement is worth more than the 'equal or lesser value' threshold, the difference is added to your transferred assessed value instead of the value resetting entirely.

faq.q: How many times can I use Prop 19?
faq.a: Eligible homeowners 55 and older or severely disabled can use the base year value transfer up to three times, and the replacement can be anywhere in California.
No. You file a claim, such as form BOE-19-B, with the assessor in the county where your new home is located, generally within three years of buying it.

body_html:
Here's a conversation I have with homeowners in their late fifties and sixties all the time. The kids are grown, the house has more bedrooms than anyone uses, and the stairs aren't getting easier. They'd love to move somewhere smaller, closer to family, or closer to the coast. Then they stop themselves: "But my property taxes would triple."

For a lot of long-time Southern California owners, that fear is what keeps them in a house that no longer fits. The good news is that California's Proposition 19 was built for exactly this situation. If you're 55 or older, it may let you take much of your existing tax base with you to a new home. Here's how it works in plain English, and how it fits into the financing side of a move.

What Prop 19 actually does

Under Proposition 13, your property tax is based on your home's assessed value, which generally starts at the purchase price and can only rise by a limited amount each year. If you bought decades ago, your assessed value may be a fraction of what the home is worth today. Normally, selling and buying a new home resets that assessed value to the new purchase price.

Prop 19, which applies to sales and purchases on or after April 1, 2021, lets eligible homeowners transfer their existing assessed value (called the "base year value") to a replacement home. According to the California State Board of Equalization (BOE), the key features are:

  • Who qualifies: homeowners 55 or older when the original home is sold, severely disabled homeowners of any age, and victims of a Governor-declared wildfire or natural disaster whose home was substantially damaged.
  • Where you can go: anywhere in California. The old county-by-county limits no longer apply.
  • How often: up to three times for the age and disability programs.
  • What qualifies: both homes must be your principal residence, and the replacement must be bought or newly built within two years of selling the original.
  • How to claim it: file the claim form (BOE-19-B for the age-based transfer) with the assessor in the county where the new home is located, within three years of buying it.

The "equal or lesser value" test and buying up

This is the part most people have never heard explained clearly. Before Prop 19, moving with your tax base generally meant buying a less expensive home. Now you can buy a home worth more, but the difference gets added to your transferred value.

The BOE's Prop 19 questions and answers describe how "equal or lesser value" is measured against the market value of the home you sold:

When you buy the replacementCounts as "equal or lesser" if it's worth up to
Before you sell the original100% of the original's market value
Within the first year after the sale105% of the original's market value
Within the second year after the sale110% of the original's market value

Here's a simplified, hypothetical illustration of the BOE's approach. Say your current home would sell for $1,000,000 and its assessed value is $350,000. If you buy a replacement for $900,000, your assessed value stays at roughly $350,000. If you instead buy a $1,200,000 home before selling, the $200,000 difference is added, so your new assessed value would be around $550,000. That's still far below a full reset to $1,200,000.

Your county assessor makes the final call on values and eligibility, and the details can get technical. Treat this as an overview, and talk with the assessor's office and a tax professional before you make decisions based on it.

Where the mortgage fits in

Prop 19 handles the tax side. The financing side is where I come in, and it's where a lot of moves get stuck. Most downsizers I talk with have significant equity but don't want to sell first, move twice, and rent in between. A few common ways to structure the move:

  1. Sell first, then buy. The simplest path. Your sale proceeds fund the next purchase, and the 105% and 110% windows give you some room to buy a little more home after you sell.
  2. Buy first with temporary financing. Bridge loans and similar tools can let you use equity in your current home before it sells. I walked through those options in Buy Before You Sell: Bridge Loans and Other Options.
  3. Buy with a new mortgage, even with plenty of equity. Some buyers prefer to keep cash in reserve rather than put everything into the next house. Lenders look at income and assets, including retirement accounts, so retirees can often qualify in ways they don't expect.
  4. Buy with a reverse mortgage for purchase. For borrowers 62 and older, an FHA-insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage can be used to buy a home without required monthly mortgage payments, though you still pay taxes, insurance, and upkeep. It isn't right for everyone, but it's worth understanding.

Timing matters for both the tax rules and the loan. Remember that buying before you sell means the 100% threshold applies, so a more expensive replacement adds more to your assessed value. That trade-off is worth running through with real numbers before you write an offer.

Common mistakes I see

  • Assuming the new home must be cheaper. It doesn't, though buying up adds to your assessed value.
  • Forgetting about occupancy. The replacement has to be your principal residence. A second home or rental doesn't qualify. If that distinction is fuzzy, read Second Home vs. Investment Property: Why Occupancy Matters.
  • Missing the claim. The transfer isn't automatic. You have to file with the assessor in the new home's county.
  • Waiting too long to buy. The two-year window runs from the sale of your original home.
  • Expecting the first tax bill to be right. Assessors may issue supplemental bills before the claim is processed. Keep paperwork handy and follow up.
  • Mixing it up with the parent-child rules. Prop 19 also changed how property passes from parents to children. That's a separate set of rules with its own requirements.

A simple game plan for a Prop 19 move

If you're 55 or older and thinking about a move, here's the order I'd suggest:

  1. Look up your current assessed value on your tax bill or your county assessor's site.
  2. Get a realistic sense of your home's market value from a local agent.
  3. Read your county's guidance. In the Inland Empire, for example, the San Bernardino County Assessor has a Prop 19 FAQ, and Orange County posts the BOE-19-B claim form online.
  4. Talk with a tax professional about your specific situation, including capital gains on the sale.
  5. Meet with a loan officer early to decide whether to sell first, buy first, or use a bridge or reverse mortgage option.
  6. Close, move in, and file your claim promptly.

The takeaway

If property taxes are the main thing keeping you in a home that no longer fits, Prop 19 may change the math more than you think. Eligible homeowners can move anywhere in California, up to three times, and keep much of their tax base, even when buying a home that costs somewhat more.

The tax rules and the loan strategy work best when they're planned together. If you're weighing a move, I'm happy to walk through your financing options so you can see the full picture before you list.
